lesson.title: Losing Yourself in the Crowd
lesson.summary: A psychological state, often triggered by anonymity and immersion in a group, in which people become less focused on their individual identity and more responsive to the norms and emotions of the group around them.
lesson.body:
Deindividuation describes a shift that can happen to people inside a crowd or a group, especially when they feel anonymous: their sense of themselves as a distinct individual, accountable for their own choices, fades into the background, and their behavior becomes governed more by the group's mood and norms than by their own private standards. This builds directly on conformity and social norms, but takes the idea further. Deindividuation is not just going along with a norm you are aware of, it is a state where the very awareness of yourself as separate from the group is reduced, which can make group norms, whatever they happen to be in that moment, unusually powerful.

The idea has deep historical roots in the writing of Gustave Le Bon, a nineteenth century thinker whose 1895 book on crowd psychology proposed that people in crowds lose their individual rational judgment and become swept up in a kind of primitive group mind. Le Bon's ideas were influential but were not developed through controlled scientific research, and modern psychologists treat them as a historically important but scientifically unsupported starting point rather than an established finding. The concept became a genuine subject of experimental psychology largely through the work of Philip Zimbardo, whose 1969 study found that participants who were made anonymous, dressed in hoods and oversized lab coats and never addressed by name, delivered longer shocks to a supposed victim than participants who kept their own identity visible and were addressed by name.

More recent research has refined rather than simply confirmed the classic picture. The social identity model of deindividuation effects, developed by researchers including Stephen Reicher, Russell Spears, and Tom Postmes, argues that anonymity does not just strip away self control and unleash primitive impulses. Instead, it shifts a person's attention away from their personal identity and toward whatever group identity is salient at the time, which makes them more responsive, not less, to the specific norms of that group in that situation. That reframing matters because it explains why deindividuation can produce very different outcomes depending on context: a crowd whose norm is hostility can turn uglier when its members feel anonymous, while a crowd whose norm is generosity or solidarity can become more generous or unified under the same anonymous conditions.

The concept is often invoked to explain behavior in large protest crowds, sports riots, and anonymous online spaces, where people sometimes act in ways they likely would not as identifiable individuals. It is worth being cautious about over simplifying these real world cases, since crowd and online behavior are shaped by many factors beyond anonymity alone, including the specific norms present, prior beliefs, and the actions of a few highly visible individuals who can set the tone for everyone else.
